newsitem.title: USA: NYC might have "biggest ever" surplus - comptroller.
newsitem.headline: NYC might have "biggest ever" surplus - comptroller.

text.p: The New York City Comptroller said Wednesday that bigger tax collections and a positive balance at the Board of Education could give the city its "biggest ever" surplus of at least $700 million.

City Comptroller Alan Hevesi said in a statement that the possibility of a record surplus, which would surpass the $570 million level hit in 1985 and 1992, was confirmed by the city now having $1 billion more in cash than it did last year.
The city's general fund had $2.16 billion in cash on April 25, substantially above last year's total of $1.05 billion.

In addition to an extra $150 million of tax revenues, the city got $75 million of debt service relief from the Municipal Assistance Corporation for the City of New York. The city had not expected to get this benefit until fiscal 1998, but instead it will be counted in fiscal 1997, which ends June 30.

And the Board of Education has a $75 million surplus. City officials, who declined to be named, have said the Giuliani Administration does not plan to take those funds away. However, the city comptroller noted that the Board has asked for $450 million more than projected in its 1998 budget.

Hevesi, a Democrat, said the surplus gives Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, a Republican, the ability to increase spending in a variety of areas -- and to shore up the city's balance sheet. "In addition to giving the city the freedom to deal with important problems, such as improving schools and reducing taxes that hinder job growth, some of the money should also be used to reduce the large budget gap in fiscal year 1998."

He added that overtime spending remains a concern, projecting it could be $30 million more than expected. The city's workforce, however, was anticipated to be 2,550 less than expected in the 1997 fiscal plan.
